content: Interventions for the treatment of pityriasis versicolor include various antifungal therapies aimed at eradicating the causative organism, Malassezia species, and preventing recurrence. Topical antifungal agents, such as azoles (e.g., ketoconazole, clotrimazole, miconazole) and allylamines (e.g., terbinafine), are commonly used as first-line treatments. These agents are applied directly to the affected areas of the skin and work by inhibiting fungal cell membrane synthesis, leading to fungal cell death. Selenium sulfide and zinc pyrithione shampoos or lotions are also effective topical options. These agents reduce fungal colonization on the skin and are often used in cases where large areas are affected. For more extensive or recurrent cases, systemic antifungal medications, such as oral azoles (e.g., fluconazole, itraconazole, ketoconazole), may be prescribed. These drugs are absorbed into the bloodstream and delivered to the skin, providing a more comprehensive treatment approach. Adjunctive measures, such as maintaining proper skin hygiene and avoiding excessive sweating or oily skin products, are recommended to reduce the risk of recurrence. In cases of hyperpigmentation or hypopigmentation caused by the condition, it is important to note that skin discoloration may persist for weeks to months after successful treatment, as the pigmentation changes are due to the effects of the fungus on melanocytes rather than active infection. Regular follow-up and, in some cases, prophylactic antifungal therapy may be necessary to prevent relapses, particularly in individuals with a history of frequent recurrences or predisposing factors such as a humid climate or immunosuppression.
